# SPINAL EPIDURAL ABSCESS

Most cases are associated with Staphylococcus aureus. Others are associated with Gram-negative bacilli and streptococci. Beta-lactam antibiotics are more effective than vancomycin against susceptible Staphylococci. If Staphylococcus is isolated, once methicillin-resistance is ruled out, switch to an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam antibiotic. Pseudomonas is a potential pathogen in post-surgical patients or patients with known Pseudomonas colonization.

# Consult Neurosurgery, Neurology, and Infectious Disease

# Duration of Therapy

Treat for 4 to 8 weeks. Shorter durations may be used in patients who have undergone surgical drainage and who have responded well to therapy.

---

References:

- Krishnamohan et al, Curr Infect Dis Rep, 2014, 16(11)1-6
- Mandell chapter: Subdural Empyema, Epidural Abscess, and Suppurative
- Up-To-Date Article: Spinal Epidural Abscess
Therapy:
## Empiric Treatment

Preferred if Pseudomonas is not suspected:

Ceftriaxone 2 gm IV q12h ($) M <AND> vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) R

Preferred if Pseudomonas is suspected:

Cefepime 2gm IV Q8h ($$) R  < AND > vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) R

Alternative:

Assessment of beta-lactam reaction

Meropenem 2 gm IV q8h ($$) R,O <AND> vancomycin 15mg/kg IV q12h ($) R

## Treatment if methicillin-sensitive S. aureus is isolated

Nafcillin 2 gm IV q4h ($$) R,DI

< OR >
Cefazolin 2 gm IV q8h ($) R
